extracted.intended_audience: aspiring cartoonists and humorists (particularly single-panel/New Yorker-style cartoonists)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for creating single‑panel cartoons that turn personal anxieties into humor in the style of Roz Chast—covering emotional core, specificity, visual grounding, tone, themes, and production workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there an anxious emotional core?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there an anxious emotional core? (Core Aesthetic: Storyteller hunting for the "sweet spot where the ridiculous and the uncomfortable converge." A good joke needs an emotional aspect.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The cartoon should be driven by an identifiable emotion (anxiety/fear/embarrassment) rather than only by a punchline or gag. Aim for the tension between the ridiculous and the uncomfortable; emotional truth anchors the humor and makes the absurdity resonate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the cartoon name a specific neurosis?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the cartoon name a specific neurosis?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity matters: name or show a precise neurotic thought or habit (the "precise neurotic thought is named") rather than vague anxiety. Concrete, idiosyncratic details help readers recognize themselves and increase comedic impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the visual cluttered/domestic to ground the absurd?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the visual cluttered/domestic to ground the absurd?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interior/domestic settings (cluttered rooms, lamps, accentuated wallpaper) to anchor surreal or anxious situations. Visual clutter grounds the joke in everyday reality and contrasts with the absurdity of the thought, increasing comedic friction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the reader feel "seen"?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful cartoons generate recognition—readers (especially anxious ones) should identify with the thought or situation. Achieve this through specificity, truthful emotional detail, and tone that signals empathy rather than judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is there subversion without confrontation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be subversive in perspective or irony but avoid direct hostility or preachiness. Influence note: work can be "subversive without being directly confrontational" (à la Charles Addams). The satire should undermine expectations quietly rather than attacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use personal anxieties as source material
rubrics_metrics.description: Pours all her "anxieties, fears, superstitions, failures, furies, insecurities, and dark imaginings — the kit and caboodle of her psyche" into her work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mine your own life and inner monologues for material. Authentic personal detail—even the darker, embarrassing stuff—creates emotional truth and unique comedic angles. Emphasize internal thoughts and private worries as the joke's fuel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: self-mockery / being first to laugh at your fears
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-mockery: she's first to laugh at her own fears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a self-deprecating stance so the humor feels invitational. By laughing at herself first, the cartoonist disarms the subject, invites reader empathy, and reduces mean-spiritedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing style and drawn texture (hand-lettered, looser)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand-lettered, looser drawing style; drawn texture: imperfection signals "real."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a loose, hand‑lettered line and visible texture over slick perfection. Imperfect marks communicate honesty and personality; the visual voice should match the neurotic, lived-in tone of the writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Themes to explore (existential dread, neurotic interior monologues, aging parents, modern anxieties, catastrophizing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Themes: existential dread; neurotic interior monologues; aging parents; modern anxieties; catastrophizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These recurring thematic territories are fertile ground. Picking a recognizable life-stage or worry (e.g., caregiving/aging parents) and amplifying its internal monologue can produce both pathos and laughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workflow/productivity and revision practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Submits 6–8 cartoons per week to The New Yorker; magazine picks at most one; keeps "rejects" in file cabinets; sometimes redraws and resubmits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat cartooning as high-volume work: produce many ideas, expect low acceptance rates, keep rejected pieces (for future reworking), and be willing to redraw/resubmit. Persistence and output volume are part of the craft.
